body.heading: More than just being tired
paragraphs: A yawn is a reflex: your mouth opens wide, you take a slow, deep breath in, and then you breathe out. People often link yawning with sleepiness or boredom, and it does tend to happen more when we are tired or under-stimulated.

But tiredness is not the whole story. People also yawn when they wake up, before a big moment, and sometimes when they are concentrating. That mix is why researchers treat yawning as a clue about the brain, not just a sign of needing bed.

body.heading: Cooling the brain, waking the body
paragraphs: One leading idea is that yawning helps regulate the temperature of the brain. A deep breath brings in cooler air and changes blood flow, which may help the brain stay in its comfortable working range.

Yawning also seems to raise alertness for a short while. Stretching the jaw and taking in more air can make a drowsy person feel briefly more awake, which may be why a yawn often arrives right when you are trying to pay attention.

body.heading: Why yawns spread
paragraphs: Seeing, hearing, or even reading about a yawn can trigger one — this is called contagious yawning. It tends to appear in children around the age of four or five, and it is stronger between people who know each other well.

Some researchers connect contagious yawning with empathy and social communication: we unconsciously mirror the people around us. The link is still debated, but the effect is real enough that you may have yawned while reading this.

takeaway: Yawning is a built-in reflex that may help cool the brain and sharpen alertness — and catching one from someone else is a normal part of being social.
